html:
The imperial mosque built by Mimar Sinan for Sultan Selim II on a hilltop in Edirne, the old Ottoman capital, from 1568 or 1569 to 1574 or 1575. Selim, the son of Suleiman the Magnificent, had governed the city as a prince and chose it over Istanbul. The mosque and its endowment were paid for partly from his share of the spoils of the conquest of Cyprus, completed with the fall of Famagusta in 1571. Selim died in December 1574, before it was finished. Sinan called it his masterpiece.

A courtyard and a prayer hall of equal size, each about 60 by 44 m, make up the main building. Inside, a single dome 31.28 m wide and about 42 m high rests on eight pillars set into the walls, so that almost nothing stands between the visitor and the dome. Sinan's biography has him boast of a dome higher and wider than that of Hagia Sophia; it is about the same width and slightly higher. Four identical minarets, about 71 m tall, among the tallest the Ottomans built, stand at the corners of the hall and frame the dome. Look for the Iznik tiles around the mihrab, set in a deep apse lit from three sides, the carved marble minbar, and the painted wooden muezzins' platform under the centre of the dome.

The mosque stands in a walled complex with two madrasas, one of them now a museum. Baháʼu'lláh, held in Edirne by the Ottomans, came here often from 1865 to 1868. In the war of 1877 to 1878 tiles from the sultan's loge were taken to Moscow, and in the siege of 1913, during the Balkan Wars, shells hit the dome; Atatürk ordered the damage left unrepaired as a reminder. The complex was listed by UNESCO in 2011.
